entities.summary:
Gaius Valerius Catullus (c. 83 BCE, Verona – c. 53 BCE), an innovative Roman lyric poet, stands as a pivotal figure in the development of Latin literature, renowned for his intense, often autobiographical verses that broke from traditional epic forms. A leading exponent of the 'neoteric' movement, Catullus championed a style emphasizing learnedness, brevity, and personal emotion over grand historical narratives. His work offers an unparalleled window into the social and emotional landscape of the late Roman Republic, capturing the complexities of love, friendship, political satire, and personal anguish in an era of profound societal change and imperial expansion.

Catullus's extant corpus, known as the *Carmina*, comprises approximately 116 poems of varying lengths and meters, collected posthumously. These include short, epigrammatic pieces (*nugae*), longer poems (*carmina maiora*), and scathing invectives. His most famous works chronicle a tumultuous affair with a woman he calls 'Lesbia,' widely identified as Clodia Metelli, a prominent Roman matron. These poems, oscillating between ecstatic devotion and bitter betrayal, established a new paradigm for Latin love poetry, exploring psychological depth and raw emotion previously unattempted. Beyond romance, Catullus engaged with political figures like Julius Caesar, reflected on personal grief, and celebrated the bonds of friendship, often with a biting wit and sophisticated literary allusions.
